notes.definition: Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials. Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation; an irradiated object does not become radioactive.
explanation: Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. For example, radioactive dust may settle on skin or clothing, or radioactive material may be breathed in or swallowed. The hazard from contamination comes from the decay of the contaminating atoms: as long as they are there, they keep emitting radiation. Contamination is hard to remove, and if the atoms are inside the body the person is exposed until the material decays or leaves the body.

Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation from a source outside it. Once the source is removed or shielded, the exposure stops. An irradiated object does not become radioactive. This is why food and medical equipment can be sterilised with gamma rays and are then safe to use: the radiation kills microorganisms but leaves nothing radioactive behind.

The type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard. Outside the body, alpha is the least dangerous, because it cannot pass through the dead outer layer of skin; beta and gamma are more dangerous because they can penetrate the body and reach organs. Inside the body, alpha is the most dangerous, because it is strongly ionising and all its energy is absorbed by the cells close to it, damaging them. Gamma is less hazardous inside the body because most of it passes straight out.

Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against the hazards of radioactive sources. These include keeping exposure time as short as possible, keeping as far from the source as possible (using tongs to handle it), using shielding such as lead-lined boxes and lead screens, wearing gloves and protective clothing to avoid contamination, and wearing dosimeters (such as film badges) to monitor the dose received by workers.

It is important for the results of studies on the effects of radiation on humans to be published and shared with other scientists. Other scientists can then check the findings through peer review, repeat the studies, and look for errors or bias. This makes sure that safety guidelines are based on reliable evidence.
keyFacts: Contamination: unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials.
The hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
Irradiation: exposing an object to nuclear radiation from an outside source.
An irradiated object does not become radioactive.
The type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard.
Outside the body: beta and gamma are most hazardous; alpha is stopped by the skin.
Inside the body: alpha is most hazardous because it is strongly ionising and absorbed by nearby cells.
Precautions: minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding, use tongs and gloves, wear a dosimeter.
Results of studies on radiation effects should be published and peer reviewed.

keyTerms.definition: The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials.
Exposing an object to nuclear radiation from an outside source; the object does not become radioactive.
The removal of electrons from atoms by radiation, which can damage cells and DNA.
Material such as lead or concrete placed between a source and people to absorb radiation.
A device, such as a film badge, worn to measure how much radiation a person has been exposed to.
The checking of scientific work by other independent scientists before or after publication.

workedExamples.title: Comparing hazards inside and outside the body
workedExamples.question: A worker handles two sources: an alpha emitter and a gamma emitter. Which is more hazardous if (a) held near the body, (b) swallowed?
steps: (a) Outside the body, alpha is stopped by the outer layer of skin, so it does little harm. Gamma penetrates the body and can reach organs. Gamma is more hazardous.
(b) Inside the body, alpha is absorbed by nearby cells and is strongly ionising, causing a lot of local damage. Most gamma passes out of the body. Alpha is more hazardous.

workedExamples.title: Is irradiated food radioactive?
workedExamples.question: Strawberries are irradiated with gamma rays to kill bacteria. Explain whether they are safe to eat afterwards.
steps: Irradiation exposes the food to radiation from an outside source.
No radioactive atoms are transferred to the food.
Irradiated objects do not become radioactive, so the strawberries emit no radiation.
workedExamples.answer: Yes: they are not radioactive, and the bacteria have been killed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think anything exposed to radiation becomes radioactive.
misconceptions.right: In fact irradiated objects do not become radioactive. Only contamination (radioactive atoms on or in the object) makes an object emit radiation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alpha is always the least dangerous radiation.
misconceptions.right: In fact alpha is the least dangerous outside the body, but the most dangerous inside the body because it is strongly ionising.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that contamination stops as soon as you move away from the source.
misconceptions.right: In fact contamination travels with you; the radioactive atoms keep decaying until they are removed or have decayed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think washing an irradiated object removes radiation from it.
misconceptions.right: In fact an irradiated object has no radioactive material to remove. Washing helps with contamination, not irradiation.

realWorld: Gamma irradiation is used to sterilise single-use medical equipment, such as syringes and surgical gloves, inside sealed packaging.
After the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents, radioactive dust contaminated land, crops and water over a large area.
Workers in nuclear power stations and hospital radiology departments wear dosimeters to monitor their exposure.
examTips: Use the exact definitions: contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms; irradiation is exposure to radiation.
Always say whether you are describing the hazard inside or outside the body; alpha changes from least to most hazardous.
When asked for precautions, give a reason for each (for example, tongs increase distance, so less radiation reaches the hands).
For questions on sharing results, mention peer review and checking findings.
summary: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in other materials.
Irradiation is exposure to radiation; the object does not become radioactive.
Contamination is usually more hazardous because exposure continues.
Outside the body beta and gamma are most dangerous; inside the body alpha is most dangerous.
Precautions: time, distance, shielding, protective clothing and monitoring; results should be peer reviewed.

questions.question: What is meant by radioactive contamination?
options: Exposing an object to radiation from a source
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials
The splitting of a large nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials
questions.explanation: Contamination means radioactive atoms have got onto or into something. Exposure from a source is irradiation.

questions.question: What is irradiation?
options: Exposing an object to nuclear radiation
Removing radioactive atoms from an object
Radioactive dust landing on an object
markScheme: 1 mark: Exposing an object to nuclear radiation
questions.explanation: Irradiation is exposure to nuclear radiation. It does not make the object radioactive. Dust landing on an object is contamination.

What happens to the food?
markScheme: 1 mark: It does not become radioactive
questions.explanation: Irradiated objects do not become radioactive. No radioactive atoms are added.

questions.question: Which type of radiation is the most hazardous if a source is swallowed?
markScheme: 1 mark: Alpha
questions.explanation: Inside the body, alpha is absorbed by nearby cells and is strongly ionising, so it causes the most damage.

questions.question: Which type of radiation is the least hazardous when the source is outside the body?
markScheme: 1 mark: Alpha
questions.explanation: Alpha cannot pass through the outer layer of skin, so it cannot reach living cells from outside.

questions.question: Why is contamination often more hazardous than irradiation?
options: The radioactive atoms stay on or in the object and keep decaying
Irradiation only lasts for one second
Contaminated objects have a longer half-life
markScheme: 1 mark: The radioactive atoms stay on or in the object and keep decaying
questions.explanation: With contamination, the radioactive atoms remain, so exposure continues. Irradiation stops as soon as the source is removed.

questions.question: Which precaution reduces the risk of contamination when handling a radioactive source?
markScheme: 1 mark: Wearing disposable gloves
questions.explanation: Gloves stop radioactive material getting onto skin. A film badge only monitors dose, and a lead screen reduces irradiation.

questions.question: Why should the results of studies on the effects of radiation on humans be published?
options: So that the radiation dose can be reduced to zero
So that other scientists can check the findings by peer review
So that the half-life of the sources can be measured
markScheme: 1 mark: So that other scientists can check the findings by peer review
questions.explanation: Publishing lets other scientists check and repeat the work (peer review), making the evidence more reliable.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how a beta source is stored in a school laboratory.
Which hazard does the lead-lined box mainly protect against?
markScheme: 1 mark: Irradiation of people nearby
questions.explanation: Lead shielding absorbs radiation, reducing irradiation of people nearby. Gloves and careful handling protect against contamination.

questions.question: State whether an object that has been irradiated becomes radioactive.
markScheme: 1 mark: no, it does not become radioactive
questions.explanation: Irradiation does not add radioactive atoms to the object.

questions.question: Give two precautions a teacher should take when using a radioactive source in a lesson.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: handle with tongs / hold at arm's length; keep exposure time short; store in a lead-lined box when not in use; never point it at people; wash hands afterwards
questions.explanation: Each precaution reduces time, increases distance or adds shielding.

questions.question: Explain why alpha radiation is the most dangerous type of radiation if it gets inside the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: alpha is strongly ionising
1 mark: all its energy is absorbed by nearby cells, causing a lot of damage (to cells/DNA)
questions.explanation: Its short range means its energy is concentrated in a small volume of tissue.

questions.question: Explain why gamma radiation from a source outside the body is more hazardous than alpha radiation from a source outside the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: gamma can penetrate the skin and reach internal organs
1 mark: alpha is stopped by the outer (dead) layer of skin
questions.explanation: Hazard from outside depends on whether the radiation can reach living tissue.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a teacher using tongs to pick up a radioactive source.
Explain why using tongs reduces the risk to the teacher.
markScheme: 1 mark: increases the distance between the source and the hand
1 mark: so less radiation reaches the hand / prevents contamination of skin
questions.explanation: Radiation spreads out, so further away means lower exposure.

questions.question: State what causes the hazard from radioactive contamination.
markScheme: 1 mark: the decay of the contaminating (radioactive) atoms
questions.explanation: The contaminating atoms emit radiation as they decay.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how radon gas from the ground can collect inside a house.
Radon gas is radioactive and emits alpha particles.
Explain why radon gas is particularly hazardous.
markScheme: 1 mark: radon gas is breathed in, so it contaminates the lungs / is inside the body
1 mark: alpha is strongly ionising and is absorbed by lung tissue, damaging cells
questions.explanation: Radon is harmless from outside but dangerous once breathed in.

questions.question: Describe the difference between contamination and irradiation.
markScheme: 1 mark: contamination is radioactive atoms on or in an object (which keep emitting radiation)
1 mark: irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source; the object does not become radioactive
questions.explanation: The key difference is whether radioactive atoms are transferred.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a film badge worn by a hospital worker.
Explain why it is important for the worker to wear the film badge.
Suggest what should happen if the badge shows that the worker has received a high dose.
markScheme: 1 mark: the badge measures the dose of radiation the worker has received
1 mark: so it can be checked that the dose is within safe limits
1 mark: if the dose is high, the worker should stop working with radiation for a time / work practices should be investigated and improved
questions.explanation: Monitoring is only useful if action is taken when limits are approached.

questions.question: Give one use of irradiation.
markScheme: 1 mark: e.g. sterilising medical equipment / food, or treating cancer
questions.explanation: Gamma irradiation kills microorganisms without leaving the object radioactive.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of contamination?
options: A patient receiving gamma rays from an external machine
Food passing through a beam of gamma rays
A worker breathing in radioactive dust
markScheme: 1 mark: A worker breathing in radioactive dust
questions.explanation: Breathing in radioactive dust puts radioactive atoms inside the body: contamination. The others are irradiation.

questions.question: Why is a radioactive source that emits only alpha particles stored in a box but not normally in a thick lead box?
options: Alpha particles are stopped by a thin layer of material
Alpha particles are not harmful at all
Lead becomes radioactive when hit by alpha
markScheme: 1 mark: Alpha particles are stopped by a thin layer of material
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are stopped by paper or a few cm of air, so thick lead is not needed. Alpha is still hazardous if it gets inside the body.

questions.question: A worker wants to reduce the dose received from a gamma source. Which action would have the greatest effect?
options: Standing behind a thick lead screen
markScheme: 1 mark: Standing behind a thick lead screen
questions.explanation: Gamma penetrates gloves, masks and skin. Thick lead absorbs a large fraction of gamma radiation. Gloves and washing protect against contamination, not irradiation by gamma.

questions.question: What is the name of a device worn by workers to monitor their exposure to radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: Dosimeter (film badge)
questions.explanation: A dosimeter, such as a film badge, records the radiation dose a worker receives over time.

questions.question: After a nuclear accident, radioactive dust lands on farmland. Explain why the crops grown there may be a hazard to people who eat them.
markScheme: 1 mark: the crops become contaminated with radioactive atoms (taken up from the soil/dust)
1 mark: eating them puts radioactive atoms inside the body, where they keep decaying and damaging cells
questions.explanation: This is contamination: the radioactive material is transferred into food and then into the body.

questions.question: Compare the hazards of contamination and irradiation.
markScheme: Indicative content: contamination means radioactive atoms on/in the object or person; exposure continues until atoms removed or decayed; can be spread to other places; hard to remove; inside the body alpha most dangerous; irradiation is exposure from an outside source; stops when source removed or shielded; object does not become radioactive; outside the body beta and gamma most hazardous, alpha stopped by skin.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison of both, including duration of exposure and the effect of radiation type.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct definitions or simple statements with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Comparison words matter: continues versus stops, inside versus outside, becomes radioactive versus does not.

questions.question:
A scientist works with three radioactive sources, X, Y and Z.
Table 1 shows the type of radiation emitted by each source.
Evaluate the hazards from each source, considering both irradiation and contamination.
Describe the precautions the scientist should take.
markScheme: Indicative content: alpha: little hazard from irradiation as stopped by skin/air; very hazardous if contamination gets inside body (inhaled or swallowed) as strongly ionising; beta: moderate hazard from outside, penetrates skin a little; moderate hazard inside; gamma: greatest irradiation hazard as it penetrates the body; less hazardous inside as much passes out, but still harmful; precautions: use tongs (distance), minimise time, store in lead-lined boxes and use shielding especially for gamma, wear gloves/protective clothing and wash hands to avoid contamination, do not eat or drink in the lab, wear a dosimeter; justified conclusion, e.g. gamma source needs most shielding, alpha source most care to avoid contamination.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed evaluation of all three sources for both irradiation and contamination, with precautions linked to the hazards and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some correct comparison of hazards and relevant precautions with partial linking.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about hazards or precautions.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Link each precaution to the hazard it reduces: shielding for gamma irradiation, gloves and hygiene for alpha contamination.
